name: Quicksort
statement: Sort a list fast by picking a pivot and partitioning everything around it, then recursing.
statementAccent: picking a pivot and partitioning everything around it
meaning: Quicksort is an efficient, general-purpose sorting algorithm based on the divide-and-conquer strategy. To sort an array, it chooses one element as a pivot and partitions the other elements into two groups, those less than the pivot and those greater than it, so that the pivot ends up in its correct final position with all smaller elements before it and all larger elements after it. It then recursively applies the same procedure to the two subarrays on either side of the pivot, and because each partitioning step places the pivot correctly, the whole array becomes sorted when the recursion reaches subarrays of size one. Quicksort was developed by the British computer scientist Tony Hoare in 1959, while he was a visiting student at Moscow State University, and published in 1961. It is an in-place sort, requiring only a small amount of additional memory, though it is not stable, meaning it does not necessarily preserve the relative order of equal elements. Its performance depends on the choice of pivot: on average it runs in order n log n time, which makes it very fast in practice, but in the worst case, such as an already-sorted array with a poor pivot choice, it degrades to order n squared. Common partitioning schemes include those due to Hoare and to Lomuto. Because of its speed, quicksort is one of the most widely used sorting algorithms, and practical implementations, such as introsort in the C++ standard library, combine it with other methods to guarantee good worst-case behaviour.
mechanism: Quicksort sorts by divide and conquer, breaking the problem of sorting an array into smaller sorting problems around a chosen pivot. The core operation is partitioning: an element is selected as the pivot, and the array is rearranged so that all elements less than the pivot come before it and all elements greater come after, leaving the pivot in its final sorted position. This is done in place, by scanning and swapping elements, using schemes such as Lomuto's, which keeps a boundary index and swaps smaller elements forward, or Hoare's original scheme, which works inward from both ends. Once partitioned, the array is split at the pivot into a left subarray of smaller elements and a right subarray of larger ones, and quicksort is called recursively on each; the base case is a subarray of zero or one element, which is already sorted. The efficiency of the whole depends on how evenly the pivot divides the array. When pivots are close to the median, the array halves at each level and there are about log n levels of order n work each, giving order n log n on average. When pivots are consistently extreme, the partitions are lopsided, the recursion is deep, and the running time degrades to order n squared, the classic bad case being sorted or reverse-sorted input with a first- or last-element pivot. Practical implementations mitigate this by choosing pivots cleverly, such as median-of-three or randomized selection, and by switching to other algorithms; introsort begins with quicksort and falls back to heapsort if the recursion grows too deep, guaranteeing order n log n worst case, which is why quicksort variants underlie standard-library sorts.

examples.text: The pivot is placed so smaller elements come before it and larger after, fixing its final position.
Quicksort recurses on the two subarrays either side of the pivot until they have one element.
Balanced pivots give order n log n on average; consistently extreme pivots degrade it to order n squared.

variants.name: Partitioning schemes
variants.text: Hoare's original two-pointer scheme and Lomuto's boundary-index scheme are the two standard partitioning methods.

variants.name: Introsort
variants.text: A hybrid that starts with quicksort and switches to heapsort when recursion is too deep, guaranteeing order n log n.

whyItMatters: Quicksort is one of the most important and widely used sorting algorithms in the history of computing, prized for being fast, simple, and memory-efficient. Sorting is among the most common operations computers perform, and quicksort's average order n log n running time, combined with its in-place operation and small constant factors, makes it the practical method of choice for enormous numbers of applications; variants of it lie at the heart of standard-library sort routines in many programming languages. It is also a canonical example in the teaching of algorithms, a clean and elegant illustration of the divide-and-conquer paradigm, of recursion, and of the difference between average-case and worst-case analysis, and its behaviour motivated deep ideas in the analysis of algorithms and in randomization, since choosing pivots at random makes the bad case vanishingly unlikely. Developed by Tony Hoare in 1959 and published in 1961, it was recognized as one of the ten algorithms with the greatest influence on science and engineering in the twentieth century. As the fast sorting method that works by picking a pivot and partitioning around it, quicksort is a cornerstone of computer science.

working.text: select one element of the array as the pivot around which to partition.
rearrange so smaller elements come before the pivot and larger after, fixing the pivot's place.
apply quicksort to the left and right subarrays until each has one element and the array is sorted.

limits: Quicksort is fast and widely used, but several points reward care. Its worst-case running time is order n squared, not order n log n; the order n log n figure is the average case, and naive implementations hit the worst case on already-sorted or reverse-sorted input when the pivot is chosen as the first or last element. Practical implementations avoid this with randomized or median-of-three pivot selection, or by switching algorithms, as introsort does. Quicksort is in place, using only order log n extra space for the recursion, but it is not stable, so equal elements may be reordered, which matters when sorting records by a key; mergesort is the usual stable alternative. The algorithm's performance also depends on implementation details and the partitioning scheme, and comparisons of Hoare's and Lomuto's schemes should not be conflated. Some historical details reward care: Hoare developed quicksort in 1959 and published it in 1961, and the divide-and-conquer structure is what it shares with mergesort, though the two differ in where the work is done. So quicksort robustly sorts by partitioning around pivots, understood as an average-case order n log n, in-place but unstable algorithm whose worst case must be guarded against.
misreadings: Quicksort is not guaranteed order n log n; that is its average case, and a poor pivot on sorted input gives order n squared. It is not stable, so it may reorder equal elements, unlike mergesort. And it is not a single fixed procedure but depends on pivot choice and partitioning scheme, so treating its worst case as n log n, assuming it preserves the order of equal keys, or ignoring the role of pivot selection, misreads it.
origin: The divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm developed by Tony Hoare in 1959 and published in 1961, which sorts by choosing a pivot, partitioning elements around it, and recursing on the two sides.
